![LLMs have internal answer distributions about user queries. Rather than just sampling one output (possibly combined with a percentage or a verbalized hedge), an LLM should generate a string that is self-reflective of its internal distribution, summarizing all plausible answers and their relative likelihoods. Figure 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](cover.png){fig-align="center"}

In *SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?* (ICLR 2026) [[1]](#ref-1), [Michael Kirchhof](https://mkirchhof.github.io/) et al. at Apple and the Tübingen AI Center introduce an information-theoretic metric for evaluating whether a single text summary a large language model (LLM) writes about its own uncertainty actually matches the distribution of answers the same model would produce if sampled many times.

> The common approach to communicate a large language model's (LLM) uncertainty is to add a percentage number or a hedging word to its response. But is this all we can do? Instead of generating a single answer and then hedging it, an LLM that is fully transparent to the user needs to be able to reflect on its internal belief distribution and output a summary of all options it deems possible, and how likely they are. To test whether LLMs possess this capability, we develop the ***SelfReflect metric*, an information-theoretic distance between a given summary and a distribution over answers*. In interventional and human studies, we find that *SelfReflect indicates even slight deviations*, yielding a fine measure of faithfulness between a summary string and an LLM's actual internal distribution over answers. With SelfReflect, we make a resounding negative observation: *modern LLMs are, across the board, incapable of revealing what they are uncertain about, neither through reasoning, nor chains-of-thoughts, nor explicit finetuning*. However, we do find that *LLMs are able to generate faithful summaries of their uncertainties if we help them by sampling multiple outputs and feeding them back into the context**. This simple approach shines a light at the universal way of communicating LLM uncertainties whose future development the SelfReflect score enables. To support the development of this universal form of LLM uncertainties, we publish the code that implements our metric for arbitrary LLMs under <https://github.com/apple/ml-selfreflect>.

## Method

How the metric works. *Input:* a candidate summary string $s$, a query $q$, and sampling access to the model $p_\theta$. *Output:* a scalar distance, lower meaning the summary is more faithful to the model's answer distribution. The paper defines a good summary $s$ as one that is *predictively sufficient* of the answer distribution $p_\theta(A \mid q)$. Intuitively, if you've read $s$, you shouldn't gain much by also reading a fresh sample from the model. Operationally, the paper turns this into a Cloze-style test. Sample $N$ answers $a_{(1:N)}$ from the model for query $q$, then take a separate sample $B$ and mask a word in it. Ask a judge LLM to predict the masked word twice: once given the candidate summary $s$ as context, once given the concatenated samples $a_{(1:N)}$ as context. Each prediction is a distribution over the vocabulary. The SelfReflect score is the **1-Wasserstein distance** between those two distributions, averaged over many masked words and queries. A summary that truly captures the answer distribution produces the same predictions as the samples do; a summary that misses facts or misweights them shifts the predicted distribution.

![How the SelfReflect metric is computed. The judge LLM is prompted twice (once with the candidate summary as context, once with the concatenated samples) and predicts a masked-out word in each case. The two predicted token distributions are compared via 1-Wasserstein distance. Figure 3 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure3.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="figure3-full.png"}

## Results

Across 20 modern LLMs tested with prompting, chain-of-thought reasoning, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and direct preference optimization (DPO), none produce summary strings that faithfully reflect their internal answer distribution. Summaries look right in form (they list possibilities and assign relative likelihoods), but the listed possibilities are not the ones the model actually samples. The fix that does work is mechanical: sample $N$ outputs from the model, feed them back as context, and ask the model to summarize *those*. The resulting summary is faithful.

In the benchmark's interventional study (taking 3 × 1,000 open-ended questions and generating known-good, known-bad, and "almost-good" summaries with Gemini 2.0 Flash), SelfReflect cleanly separates near-misses where other metrics cannot:

![Discrimination accuracy of SelfReflect and alternative benchmark metrics on pairs of good and bad summaries, across six comparison types. Higher is better (chance = 50%). SelfReflect (bottom row) achieves the highest Good-vs-almost-good accuracy at 93.2%, while traditional baselines (LM Judge, Embedding) sit near or only modestly above chance. Table 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](table1.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="table1-full.png"}

Discriminating an almost-good summary from a good one is the setting that matters for "did the LLM really convey its uncertainty?", and that is the column where the LM-judge baseline drops near chance (47.3%) and other traditional baselines do only modestly better.

## My Notes

- **The negative result matters more than the metric.** The literature on LLM self-reports has been accumulating evidence in one direction for a few years now: chain-of-thought explanations don't necessarily reflect the actual computation [[2]](#ref-2), verbalized confidence is systematically overconfident across five widely-used LLMs [[3]](#ref-3), and now text self-summaries of internal answer distributions don't match those distributions either. Each result is locally about a different self-report channel, but the pattern across them converges: when an LLM tells you something about itself, the right prior is that the statement is shaped by self-report patterns picked up from training data, not by introspection on the actual generative process. [Liu and van der Schaar's position paper on intrinsic metacognitive learning](/posts/20260430-intrinsic-metacognitive-learning/) [[5]](#ref-5) argues that genuine self-improving agents need intrinsic metacognitive capabilities, with the ingredients at least partly present in current LLMs. SelfReflect's negative result is a direct empirical bound on one facet of the metacognitive-knowledge ingredient: the ability to faithfully describe one's own answer distribution.

- **The "sample-then-summarize" workaround is the practical bottom line and it has pipeline implications.** The paper shows that LLMs can write faithful uncertainty summaries. They just need the samples in context first. That makes the missing capability not summary-writing but introspection on their own answer distribution without sampling it. For agent and product designers: if you want a calibrated multi-option response, use i.i.d. sampling plus a summarization pass. A clever prompt asking the model to "be honest about your uncertainty" won't substitute for the samples. The cost is $N$ forward passes; the upside is a summary the SelfReflect metric scores as faithful.

- **The metric is more discriminating than the alternatives.** Most evaluation work in this area has leaned on either LM-judge metrics (which have known failure modes) or coarse calibration scores (which discard structure). An information-theoretic distance between a string and a distribution (predictive sufficiency, scored against the empirical answer distribution) discriminates good from almost-good summaries where LM judges and embedding distances do not. Whether downstream work picks it up is the open question; if so, future "LLMs reveal their uncertainties" claims will need to clear a real bar rather than a vibes check.

- **Three deployment uses beyond benchmarking.** The same score plugs into several runtime loops the paper doesn't explore. As a training reward it targets the property SFT and DPO miss under naive objectives: optimize against the metric directly and you train for faithful self-summary rather than a proxy. As an ops-time ablation signal it answers "given my model and my query distribution, which prompting regime yields the most faithful uncertainty reports?", narrower than the paper's capability ranking and closer to production tuning. As a sampled monitoring signal it audits a cheaper production path (e.g., direct verbalized uncertainty) on a subset of traffic: large divergence on the sampled queries means the cheaper path has drifted, and the operator should fall back to sample-then-summarize or route to human review. Per-query routing is not a sensible use because computing SelfReflect for a query already costs the $N$ samples that sample-then-summarize would need anyway.

- **Part of a broader push to ascertain a model's epistemic status.** Whether an LLM knows a fact, and whether it can accurately describe its own uncertainty, are both aspects of what the model actually knows versus what it claims. [KGLens](/posts/20260430-kglens-knowledge-probing/) [[4]](#ref-4) targets factual knowledge by turning a knowledge graph into natural-language questions and comparing model answers to the graph's facts. SelfReflect targets self-knowledge of uncertainty by comparing a written summary to the distribution the model actually samples. Both route around the problem that LLMs produce fluent output regardless of whether they know the answer, by grounding the measurement in a signal the model can't game by sounding confident.
